## Findings

Line numbers are those of `ART.md` at the commit. Each replacement is the whole line, cell or sentence, ready to paste.

**1. The representation, "What a chamber is", line 122 (the builder's sentence).** Air reaches a room by any one way of open cells (line 121), so a wall right across one of two ways shuts no air out, and "every defence leaves a way" forbids that wall; "one cell high" also misnames a way that runs upright. Replace line 122 with:

> - A wall built right across the only open way to a room shuts the air out of it, and a room without air is no chamber. So a defence never shuts a chamber in: at least one way of open cells, however narrow, is left from the mouth to each chamber it defends, and a raider ant fits that way.

**2. The object-by-action grid, "The wrong uses", line 53.** "A wall across a tunnel" is the wall of line 122: heaped right across the only way it makes the room behind no chamber, and then no beetle comes to lean on it (line 162), so the first thing most children try has a consequence the sentence does not tell. Replace the first sentence of line 53 ("Sand set down as a wall across a tunnel ... with sand on its head.") with:

> Sand heaped as a wall in a tunnel is the first thing most children will try, and it fails in the best way, twice: heaped right to the roof it shuts the air out, and the room behind goes dim and stale and the workers leave it; with a gap left over it for the air, the first beetle leans, the wall sighs into a pile, and the beetle walks over it with sand on its head.

**3. The invaders' table, line 250, the cell "Passes" of the dung beetle with its ball.** By line 122 every wall that holds leaves a gap, so to a ball it is also a way made too narrow by sand or mud: this cell has the ball dig it wider, while the cell below has a wall that holds 6 or more stop it and line 256 has soft walls dug only while the fly is up. Replace the cell with (the test for a wall is the one of line 111, room beyond or earth behind):

> Any wall weaker than the ball's push of 6. Where earth, or sand or mud with earth or rock behind it, makes the way too narrow for the ball, it stops and digs the way wider. Lumps with room beyond them are a wall, the gap left over them for the air included: the ball leans on them and does not dig them, except while the dung fly is up.

**4. The toy, line 37 (the paste of finding 7), against lines 30 and 32 (finding 8) and lines 240 and 260 (findings 10 and 6).** A finger that lands on a lump to carry it bites "the mouthful under it" at once, two cells across, so every pick-up eats earth beside the lump for good, the floor a wall stands on included; and "a drag that starts anywhere else digs" covers a drag that starts on a machine, which lines 240 and 260 say moves the machine. Replace line 37 with:

> - **A drag that starts on a lump carries it.** A touch that lands on a lump bites nothing, not the earth beside the lump either: the lump answers as in the first column of the grid. When the ant can reach the lump by an open way it takes that one lump in its jaws, follows the finger along the open way and sets the lump down in the open cell where the finger lets go; let go where a lump cannot lie, it goes back to the cell it came from. A drag that starts on a machine moves the machine and bites nothing (see the two machines). A drag that starts anywhere else in the ground digs, and a lump it meets is answered as in the first column of the grid and is not picked up.
